one_liner: Pure-Rust thread-caching global allocator; author's harness shows 1.9-3.5x the best C allocator on mixed-size churn, parity elsewhere.
what_it_does: A general-purpose memory allocator written in Rust with no dependencies and no build script, installed with `#[global_allocator] static GLOBAL: Allox = Allox;` in place of the system allocator or the mimalloc/jemalloc crates. It also exposes allox::malloc/calloc/realloc/free, prefixed C ABI symbols (allox_malloc, allox_free, ...), stats, optional telemetry and a no_std mode, and builds for Linux, macOS, Windows, i686 and wasm32-unknown-unknown without a C toolchain.
how_it_is_fast: It follows the mimalloc design: about 12.5%-spaced size classes in 64 KiB single-class pages, per-thread free lists with no locks or atomics on the fast path, and per-class sharded global heaps reached only by batched refills (about 64 blocks per lock). Rust-specific choices add to that: GlobalAlloc frees take the size class from the Layout through a lookup table instead of loading a page header (the changelog puts that load at about 48% of free cycles on mixed-all), the fast paths are frameless leaf functions with slow paths tail-called, and growing realloc chains move once into a reserved slack region and then grow in place. Large blocks are kept in per-thread, hot and cold (madvise-discarded) region caches instead of being unmapped, which is where the large-row gains come from.
when_to_use: Rust binaries that want a faster global allocator but cannot rely on a C toolchain: cross-compilation, wasm32 (replacing dlmalloc, the wasm default) or i686, where the mimalloc, snmalloc and jemalloc crates need cc or CMake.

Allocation-heavy code that churns mixed sizes from 16 B to 64 KiB on one or a few threads: 2.6-3.5x the best of glibc, mimalloc and snmalloc at 1 thread and 1.9-3.4x at 8 threads in the author's harness.
Container growth by realloc doubling up to 1 MiB (growable extents): ecs 8T at 1.25x glibc, which uses zero-copy mremap.
Windows programs contending on HeapAlloc: 3.7-4.96x the system allocator on the small-object rows of the older Windows table.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ programs: there is no malloc/free interposition and no operator new replacement, only prefixed allox_* symbols in an rlib (Cargo.toml declares no staticlib or cdylib), and allox_malloc(0) returns null; use mimalloc, snmalloc or jemalloc there.

Many-threaded services that calloc small objects or run String/Vec/HashMap work across threads: zeroed-small 8T at 0.67x snmalloc and the 4-thread application benchmark at 0.90x snmalloc and 0.94x mimalloc.
Production use that needs maturity: single author, 1 star, explicitly not audited, API may change before 0.2, and not published on crates.io even though the README tells you to add allox = "0.1".

Memory-tight processes: it retains freed pages and regions (up to 32 MiB hot per large-region shard across 8 shards, plus per-thread stashes and discarded virtual reserves); peak RSS in the harness was 93 MiB on mixed-small 8T, 118 MiB on mixed-all 8T and about 300 MiB on prodcons 8T.

integration.dependencies: none (tikv-jemallocator is an optional bench-only feature; mimalloc, snmalloc-rs, talc and dlmalloc are dev-dependencies for the benchmarks)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.79 (MSRV, stable channel; checked in CI)
integration.platforms: Linux and other Unix, macOS, Windows, wasm32-unknown-unknown, i686; the arena-backed big tier and in-place growth are Unix+std only; no_std mode needs a supported memory backend and is meant for single-threaded targets
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe GlobalAlloc with lock-free per-thread caches and mutex-sharded global heaps; thread pools should call allox::flush_current_thread() to hand back cached blocks; no_std builds use one global cache behind a spin mutex
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — a one-line #[global_allocator] swap for Rust programs; not a malloc/free or operator new replacement for C/C++ (prefixed allox_* C ABI only, rlib only, zero-size requests return null)

gotchas: zeroed-large 1T's 86.63x is a harness artifact: for a recycled 5-8 MiB block, alloc_large_ex calls sys::discard (madvise MADV_DONTNEED) and calloc then skips its memset, but benches/alloc.rs writes only the first byte of each block, so allox pays one madvise and one page fault while glibc, mimalloc and snmalloc memset 5-8 MiB. A caller that writes the whole buffer would pay roughly 1,300-2,000 page faults with kernel zero-fill instead, a cost the benchmark never triggers. The same one-byte touch applies to every large and huge row, so those rows measure bookkeeping and memory retention, not memory traffic; snmalloc's 1-22 K/s on them works out to a near-constant 6.5-9 GB/s of block bytes (derived from page data), which suggests it touches or zeroes whole blocks on every allocation, so the large-row ratios against snmalloc reflect that behaviour and its build settings.

The direct-call harness exercises only the GlobalAlloc path, whose frees take the size class from the Layout (dealloc_with_layout) and skip the page-header load that the changelog says was about 48% of free cycles on mixed-all. C callers going through allox_free take dealloc_impl's header lookup instead, a path the published tables never measure, and glibc's free gets no size at all. Part of the mixed-size lead may come from this sized free, which C callers would not get (an inference, not measured).

scripts/app_bench.sh runs under set -o pipefail but checks the build with `if ! cargo build ... | grep -q '^error'`: when the build fails, cargo's non-zero status becomes the pipeline status, `!` makes it look like success, and the script runs whatever older binary sits in target/app-<feature>/. The 'build failed' branch is effectively unreachable, so a stale binary can be benchmarked silently. The script also runs each backend once (APP_SECS defaults to 3), so the README's 'median of 3-5 x 2 s, interleaved' protocol for the application table was done by hand and not logged.

The README says the numbers come from a shared dev box whose load average 'wanders between 2 and 12' with a ~10% run-to-run noise floor, and its size labels disagree with the code (big-tail is 262145-524289 B, big-upper-tail 524289-1048577 B, large-only 8T 32768-262144 B). Its own known-defects note says the batched telemetry counters lose their last window, so the counter-based zeroed-small analysis is unreliable.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling in this category is an allocator (they are sorts, file tools, compilers and codecs). Against mimalloc and snmalloc themselves, pick allox only for Rust targets where a C toolchain is a problem (cross-compiling, wasm32, i686) or for mixed-size churn on a few threads, and keep mimalloc or snmalloc for many-threaded production services and for any C/C++ code.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's own direct-call harness (benches/alloc.rs: every allocator called through a &'static dyn GlobalAlloc, fresh process per run, median of 3 x 2 s, Ryzen 5 1600 pinned to 8 logical CPUs, release LTO build; rustc, glibc and the comparators' C flags unstated, Cargo.lock pins mimalloc 0.1.52 and snmalloc-rs 0.7.5), allox beat the best of glibc, mimalloc and snmalloc by 1.9-3.5x on mixed-size and medium churn and by 1.25-6.3x on large rows that write one byte per block, and tied (1.02-1.12x, inside the stated noise) on fixed-size small rows. It lost zeroed-small 8T (0.67x) and the 4-thread String/Vec/HashMap application run (0.90-0.94x), and led that application run 1.06x at 1 thread.
status_note: Active but very young: the README and changelog call it v0.1.0 (2026-09-26), yet crates.io has no allox crate, so it needs a git dependency. Its 1,355 commits end in auto-numbered 'v0.0.13xx' commits and 20 docs commits that only append hidden README comments. It is MIT OR Apache-2.0 with zero dependencies, CI runs Miri, fuzzing and Kani on a schedule, and the author says it is not audited.
